etymology: From the Anglo-French amercier, “to fine,” from the phrase estre a merci, “to be at the mercy” of the court — that is, to stand liable to a penalty the judges shall set; hence to punish by a pecuniary fine.
biblical_def: To amerce is to fine — to lay a money penalty upon a wrongdoer at the discretion of the judges, who hold him at their mercy for the sum. The word occurs once in the KJV, and it stands in a law that guards a woman’s name. If a man took a wife, hated her, and then slandered her virginity to be rid of her, the elders of the city were to chastise him, “and they shall amerce him in an hundred shekels of silver, and give them unto the father of the damsel, because he hath brought up an evil name upon a virgin of Israel” (Deu 22:19). Mark the particulars. The fine is heavy — a hundred shekels, twice the bride-price of Exo 22:16 — and it is not paid to the treasury but into the hand of her house, the very house he shamed. He is scourged besides (Deu 22:18), and he forfeits forever the right to put her away. The LORD counted a woman’s good name a thing worth a court, a scourging, and a hundred shekels of silver: “A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches” (Pro 22:1), and he who steals it must pay. The law of Israel is not indifferent to the tongue. Where a man used his mouth as a weapon against the wife of his covenant, the elders sat, the truth was tried, and the slanderer was amerced. Here is the God who forbids the talebearer (Lev 19:16) and who Himself will amerce every idle word in the day of judgment.
webster_summary: To punish by a fine; to lay a pecuniary penalty upon an offender at the discretion of the court.
webster_full: AMERCE, to inflict a penalty in money; to fine; to punish by a mulct.
From a merci, “at the mercy” of the court, which sets the sum.
It differs from a fixed fine in that the amount lies with the judges.
The slanderer of a wife was amerced an hundred shekels of silver (Deu 22:19).
The silver was paid to the injured house, not to the public purse.
scriptures: And they shall amerce him in an hundred shekels of silver, and give them unto the father of the damsel, because he hath brought up an evil name upon a virgin of Israel: and she shall be his wife; he may not put her away all his days.
And the elders of that city shall take that man and chastise him;
Pro 22:1
A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold.
Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD.
corruption_summary: A word for the court’s fine, and a law worth honouring: God set a heavy price on the man who slandered his wife’s name.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a live misuse to name here, and it is the cheapening of the tongue. Our age slanders freely and pays nothing: a reputation is destroyed in an afternoon, the words are never tried before any elder, and the injured party is told to bear it. The law of Deu 22 says otherwise. When a man brought up an evil name upon his wife, the elders of the city sat, examined the matter, chastised him, and amerced him in an hundred shekels of silver — paid into the hand of her father, the house he had shamed. God does not treat a lie about a woman as a private grievance to be swallowed; He treats it as a crime with a court, a scourge, and a price.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture’s law is the real protection of a woman’s name, and it always was. The husband who hated his wife and would be rid of her by slander found the law standing between him and his design: he was fined double the bride-price and bound to keep her all his days, that no man might learn to lie his way out of a covenant. Let no one say the God of Israel was careless of daughters. He counted a good name better than great riches, and He amerced the man who stole one. The tongue that slanders now goes unfined at the city gate; it will not go unfined at the judgment seat, where every idle word is reckoned.
roots_summary: The word means to punish by a fine set at the discretion of the court.
roots_lines: Amerce — Anglo-French amercier, “to fine.”
From estre a merci, to stand “at the mercy” of the judges.
It denotes a pecuniary penalty whose sum the court appoints.
A KJV hapax: the slanderer amerced an hundred shekels (Deu 22:19).
The silver went to the house whose daughter he had defamed.
usage: They shall amerce him in an hundred shekels: God set a price on a slandered name.
The elders chastised and amerced the man; the law stood between the wife and his malice.
To amerce is to be held at the court’s mercy for the sum — and the slanderer had no plea.

etymology: From the Old French emplaidier, “to plead against, to sue,” from en (“in”) and plaid, “a plea, a suit”; hence to prosecute a man at law, to bring an action against him before a lawful court.
biblical_def: To implead is to sue — to bring a man to law, to lay a charge against him before the appointed magistrate and let the case be tried. The word occurs once in Scripture, and it falls from the lips of a pagan town clerk in Ephesus, quieting a riot. The silversmiths, led by Demetrius, had filled the theatre with two hours of shouting for Diana, and the clerk stilled them with an argument for lawful order: “if Demetrius, and the craftsmen which are with him, have a matter against any man, the law is open, and there are deputies: let them implead one another” (Act 19:38). The law is open. There are deputies. Take your grievance to the court and not to the mob. If the matter runs further, “it shall be determined in a lawful assembly” (Act 19:39). Here a heathen official states a truth Scripture teaches from the Law to the Epistles: the magistrate bears the sword as the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil (Rom 13:4), and a grievance settled by a crowd is not settled but avenged. The clerk’s common sense saved Paul’s companions that day. Yet Paul himself sets a limit upon the courts for the church: “Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints?” (1Co 6:1). Brothers who implead one another before unbelievers have already lost, whatever the verdict. The magistrate’s court restrains the world; the church’s elders should be able to judge the smallest matter between brethren.
webster_summary: To sue; to prosecute at law; to bring an action against a man before a lawful court.
webster_full: IMPLEAD, to institute and prosecute a suit against a person in court.
From Old French emplaidier, “to plead against”; the plaintiff impleads the defendant.
It supposes a lawful court, an open law, and an appointed magistrate.
The town clerk of Ephesus bade Demetrius implead rather than riot (Act 19:38).
Paul forbids brethren to implead one another before the unjust (1Co 6:1).
scriptures: Wherefore if Demetrius, and the craftsmen which are with him, have a matter against any man, the law is open, and there are deputies: let them implead one another.
But if ye enquire any thing concerning other matters, it shall be determined in a lawful assembly.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints?
corruption_summary: The old word for suing at law; it recovers lawful process against mob rule, and the church’s duty to judge its own matters.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the mob, and our generation needs the rebuke. Ephesus was full of a crowd that shouted for two hours and, as Luke drily records, the more part knew not wherefore they were come together. The town clerk did not flatter them. He told them the law was open and there were deputies, and bade them implead one another like men rather than howl like a herd. That is the magistrate’s office under God: he beareth not the sword in vain, and a grievance carried to the crowd is not justice but vengeance dressed as zeal. Where a people despises lawful process and prefers the theatre, the innocent are torn and the guilty go free, and the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the second half of the doctrine. The state’s court restrains evildoers, but the church is not to run to it with its own quarrels: “Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints?” Brethren who implead one another before unbelievers publish their shame to the world and have suffered a defeat already, whatever the verdict. Paul’s remedy is a plurality of faithful elders competent to judge the smallest matters, and hearts willing rather to take wrong. The world goes to court; the church goes to its elders, and often to the cross — for it is better to be defrauded than to drag Christ’s name before Caesar.
roots_summary: The word means to sue, to prosecute a man at law before a lawful court.
roots_lines: Implead — Old French emplaidier, “to plead against.”
From plaid, “a plea, a suit”; hence to bring an action at law.
It supposes an open law and appointed deputies to hear the cause.
A KJV hapax, on the lips of the town clerk of Ephesus (Act 19:38).
Paul forbids saints to implead one another before the unjust (1Co 6:1).
usage: The law is open, and there are deputies: let them implead one another — order against the mob.
The magistrate bears the sword as God’s minister; the crowd bears only its own wrath.
Brethren who implead each other before the unjust have lost before the verdict is read.

etymology: From the older English use of day for a day appointed for hearing a cause, hence a day’s-man — the man who sits on the appointed day: an umpire, an arbiter, a mediator empowered to judge between two parties and bind them both to his award.
biblical_def: A daysman is an umpire — the arbiter who sits on the day appointed to hear a cause, hears both parties, and lays his hand upon each to bind them to his judgment. The word occurs once in Scripture, and it is one of the deepest cries in the Old Testament. Job, crushed and misjudged, longs to bring his cause before God and knows he cannot: “For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him, and we should come together in judgment” (Job 9:32). The creature cannot summon the Creator to court; the gulf is infinite. So Job laments, “Neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both” (Job 9:33). He wants an umpire who can touch God with one hand and man with the other — one who shares the nature of each, or he can lay hold of neither. No angel will serve, for an angel is not God; no prophet will serve, for a prophet is not God either. Job’s cry is answered in the fulness of time: “there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5). Here is the daysman — true God of true God, and true man of the substance of His mother; one Person in two natures, united without confusion, without change, without division, without separation, as Chalcedon confessed. He lays one hand on God because He is God, and one hand on man because He is man, and He is not two mediators but one. “For this cause he is the mediator of the new testament” (Heb 9:15), and by His death the called receive the promise of eternal inheritance.
webster_summary: An umpire or arbiter; one who sits on an appointed day to judge between two parties — in Job, the mediator man cannot find and God has given in Christ.
webster_full: DAYSMAN, an umpire or arbiter; a mediator appointed to decide a cause.
From day, the day set for hearing, and man; the margin of Job reads “umpire.”
He lays his hand upon both parties, binding each to his award.
A KJV hapax: Job cries that no daysman stands betwixt him and God (Job 9:33).
The office is filled by the one mediator, the man Christ Jesus (1Ti 2:5).
scriptures: Job 9:33
Neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both.
Job 9:32
For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him, and we should come together in judgment.
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
Heb 9:15

And for this cause he is the mediator of the new testament, that by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance.
corruption_summary: The umpire Job could not find and God has given. Two errors assault it: the religion of direct access without a mediator, and Rome’s intruding of many mediators against Scripture’s “one.”
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the denial that any daysman is needed at all — the religion of direct access on one’s own terms, which walks into the presence of God as though no gulf were fixed and no wrath abode. Job knew better. He knew that God is not a man as he was, that they could not come together in judgment, and that without an umpire to lay a hand on both he had no standing and no hope. Every man who prays to a God he has never been reconciled to, who assumes a hearing he was never granted, is asking Job’s question and refusing Job’s answer. There is no coming to the Father but by the Son. To come without the daysman is to come without a hand to hold, and there is no other name given among men.

The second corruption runs the opposite way and is Rome’s: not too few mediators but too many. Scripture says one mediator between God and men, and Rome has interposed Mary as mediatrix, the saints as intercessors, and the priest at the altar — a whole scaffolding of daysmen erected against the plain word of 1Ti 2:5. The reason they cannot serve is the reason Chalcedon gives for why Christ can: the umpire must lay his hand upon both, and no creature, however honoured, can lay a hand on God. Mary was a sinner saved by her Son; the saints are debtors like ourselves; the priest has no blood of his own to bring. Only He who is one Person in two natures — without confusion, change, division, or separation — touches deity and humanity at once. Job asked for a daysman, and God gave him not a committee but a Christ.
roots_summary: The word means an umpire or arbiter who sits on the appointed day and binds both parties to his judgment.
roots_lines: Daysman — from day (the day appointed to hear a cause) + man.
It denotes an umpire or arbiter; the Job margin reads “umpire.”
He lays his hand upon both parties, having authority over each.
Job found no daysman betwixt himself and God (Job 9:33).
Christ fills the office: God and man in one Person (1Ti 2:5).
usage: Job cried for a daysman to lay his hand upon both — and God answered with His Son.
The daysman must touch both parties: only the God-man can reach heaven and earth at once.
One mediator, not many: the office admits of no Mary, no saint, no priest beside Christ.

etymology: From the Middle English noy, a shortening of annoy (from Old French anoier, “to vex, to injure”), with the suffix -some; hence hurtful, noxious, destructive. It has no kinship with noise: a noisome thing is not loud but deadly.
biblical_def: Noisome means noxious — hurtful, destructive, working ruin. The modern ear hears noise in it and thinks of a smell or a racket, but the word is older and graver: that is noisome which does harm, and in Scripture it always names an instrument of judgment in the hand of God. The psalm of the sheltered saint promises deliverance from it: “Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence” (Psa 91:3) — the plague that stalks unseen and kills, against which no man can arm himself, and from which only the Almighty can cover a soul with His feathers. In Ezekiel the word names one of the LORD’s four sore judgments upon a land that has trespassed: “If I cause noisome beasts to pass through the land, and they spoil it, so that it be desolate” (Eze 14:15), and again He threatens to send upon Jerusalem “the sword, and the famine, and the noisome beast, and the pestilence, to cut off from it man and beast” (Eze 14:21). Mark the grammar: I cause, I send. The beast and the plague are not loose in the world by accident; they are His servants, and He appoints their errand. Last, at the pouring of the first vial, “there fell a noisome and grievous sore upon the men which had the mark of the beast” (Rev 16:2). The word closes where it began — God’s hand, God’s judgment, and God’s people covered under His wings.
webster_summary: Noxious; hurtful; destructive — not related to noise, but to annoy.
webster_full: NOISOME, noxious to health; hurtful; mischievous; destructive.
From noy, a contraction of annoy; wholly distinct from noise.
The noisome pestilence is the plague from which God delivers His own (Psa 91:3).
The noisome beast is one of the LORD’s four sore judgments (Eze 14:21).
The first vial pours out a noisome and grievous sore (Rev 16:2).
scriptures: Psa 91:3
Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence.
If I cause noisome beasts to pass through the land, and they spoil it, so that it be desolate, that no man may pass through because of the beasts:
For thus saith the Lord GOD; How much more when I send my four sore judgments upon Jerusalem, the sword, and the famine, and the noisome beast, and the pestilence, to cut off from it man and beast?
Rev 16:2
And the first went, and poured out his vial upon the earth; and there fell a noisome and grievous sore upon the men which had the mark of the beast, and upon them which worshipped his image.
corruption_summary: An old word for the noxious; it recovers that plague and beast are God’s appointed servants, and that His own are hid under His wings.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes an age that has emptied calamity of God. When the noisome pestilence walks through a city, the modern man reaches for every cause but the first: he will name the vector, the season, the failure of the magistrate, and never once the God who says “I send.” Ezekiel gives no such comfort. The sword, the famine, the noisome beast, and the pestilence are the LORD’s four sore judgments, sent by His hand upon a land that has trespassed grievously, and they do exactly what He appoints and no more. To read a plague as bare misfortune is to be struck and never look up — to endure the rod and miss the Father who wields it, and so to waste the affliction entirely.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sheltered saint. The same providence that sends the noisome pestilence covers His own with His feathers, and under His wings shall they trust. Psalm 91 does not promise that no plague exists; it promises a Deliverer over it. The believer is not exempt from the world’s afflictions, but he is never at their mercy, for they come to him through the hand of a Father and go when that hand is lifted. And the last noisome sore falls not on the church but on the men that bear the mark of the beast. Judgment has an address, and grace has a covering.
roots_summary: The word means noxious, hurtful, destructive — from annoy, not from noise.
roots_lines: Noisome — Middle English noy, from annoy, + -some.
It means noxious, hurtful, working ruin; it has no kin to noise.
The noisome pestilence: the plague God delivers His own from (Psa 91:3).
The noisome beast: one of four sore judgments God sends (Eze 14:21).
The noisome sore of the first vial falls on the marked (Rev 16:2).
usage: Noisome means noxious, not loud: the noisome pestilence kills in silence.
“If I cause noisome beasts to pass through the land” — the beast is God’s servant, not chance.
He shall deliver thee from the noisome pestilence: the plague comes and goes at His word.

etymology: From the Old English weard, “a watching, a guard,” kin to warden and to the German Wart; hence the act of watching, the place of watching, the body of men who watch, the custody in which one is held, and the charge appointed to a man.
biblical_def: Ward is the old word for watch and custody together — the guarding, the guard, the guard-post, and the place where the guarded are kept. Scripture uses every sense. It is a prison: Pharaoh put the butler and the baker into the house of the captain of the guard, “and they continued a season in ward” (Gen 40:4), and it was there, in Joseph’s long custody, that God set the hinge of Israel’s deliverance. It is the guard-post of a jail: when the angel led Peter out, “they were past the first and the second ward” before the iron gate opened to them of his own accord (Act 12:10) — two watches and a bolted gate could not hold a man God meant to walk free. It is an appointed course of service: David’s singers cast lots “ward against ward, as well the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar” (1Ch 25:8), each house taking its turn in the courses of praise. And it is a charge in the house of God: Nehemiah cleansed the people from all strangers “and appointed the wards of the priests and the Levites, every one in his business” (Neh 13:30). So the word gathers a doctrine of ordered watchfulness. God’s house is not a crowd but a roster; every man has his ward and stands in it. The saint is himself kept in ward — not by Pharaoh but by power divine, kept through faith unto salvation. Joseph in ward and Peter past the wards preach the same LORD: the custody of men cannot hold, and the custody of God cannot fail.
webster_summary: The act of watching or guarding; a garrison or guard-post; custody or confinement; an appointed charge or course of duty.
webster_full: WARD, the act of guarding; watch; the state of being guarded.
A place of confinement; custody; a prison, as Joseph in ward (Gen 40:4).
A guard-post or station of watchmen, as the first and second ward (Act 12:10).
An appointed course or turn of service, ward against ward (1Ch 25:8).
A charge committed to a man in the house of God (Neh 13:30).
scriptures: Gen 40:4
And the captain of the guard charged Joseph with them, and he served them: and they continued a season in ward.

When they were past the first and the second ward, they came unto the iron gate that leadeth unto the city; which opened to them of his own accord: and they went out, and passed on through one street; and forthwith the angel departed from him.
And they cast lots, ward against ward, as well the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar.
Thus cleansed I them from all strangers, and appointed the wards of the priests and the Levites, every one in his business;
corruption_summary: An old word for watch, custody, and appointed charge; it recovers ordered service in God’s house and the keeping of His own.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes an age that will keep no watch and take no post. In David’s house the singers cast lots ward against ward, small and great, teacher and scholar alike, that none should be idle and none should be lord; Nehemiah appointed the wards of the priests and Levites, every one in his business. God’s house is a roster, not a mob: every member has a ward, and to stand in it faithfully when no eye sees is the whole of the duty. The modern temper wants the church without the charge — the singing without the courses, the membership without the watch. But a ward unmanned is a gate unguarded, and the flock is spoiled where the watchman sleeps.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the double custody of God. Joseph continued a season in ward, forgotten by the butler he had served, and every day of that prison was laying the foundation of a nation’s bread. Peter slept between two soldiers and walked past the first and the second ward, and the iron gate opened of his own accord. The custody of men is never final; the LORD keeps the keys of Pharaoh’s prison and Herod’s. And the saint himself is held in a better ward — kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation, a custody no gate can open and no enemy can storm.
roots_summary: The word means the act of watching, the place or body that watches, the custody held, and the charge appointed.
roots_lines: Ward — Old English weard, “a watching, a guard.”
Kin to warden and warder; the one who keeps the watch.
It denotes custody: Joseph continued a season in ward (Gen 40:4).
It denotes a guard-post: the first and the second ward (Act 12:10).
It denotes an appointed charge: ward against ward (1Ch 25:8).
usage: Joseph continued a season in ward, and God was building Egypt’s granaries all the while.
Peter passed the first and the second ward: no watch holds the man heaven means to free.
They cast lots ward against ward — in God’s house every man has his post and keeps it.

etymology: From the Old English ūtlendisc, “of a foreign land,” from ūt (“out”) and land; hence foreign, of another country. The modern sense of “bizarre” is a later drift; in the KJV it means simply foreign.
biblical_def: Outlandish in the KJV does not mean strange or absurd, as our ears now take it. It means of an out-land — foreign, belonging to another country. It occurs once, in Nehemiah’s hardest reproof. He had found men of Judah who had married wives of Ashdod, of Ammon, and of Moab, whose children could not speak the Jews’ language, and he contended with them and pressed the case with the one example none could answer: “Did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things? yet among many nations was there no king like him, who was beloved of his God… nevertheless even him did outlandish women cause to sin” (Neh 13:26). The argument is devastating. Solomon was the wisest of men, beloved of his God, unmatched among kings — and his foreign wives turned away his heart after other gods, so that his heart was not perfect with the LORD (1Ki 11:4). If wisdom itself could be dragged into idolatry through the marriage bed, what shall become of lesser men? Nehemiah’s charge is named plainly: “to transgress against our God in marrying strange wives” (Neh 13:27). It is a covenant question, not a blood question. The danger of the outlandish wife was never her ancestry but her altar — she brought Chemosh and Ashtoreth into the house, and the husband bowed. Paul says the same to the church in the language of the yoke: “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers… what communion hath light with darkness?” (2Co 6:14). The line God draws runs between faith and unbelief, and it has never run between peoples.
webster_summary: Foreign; of another land. In the KJV the plain sense is foreign, not the modern “bizarre.”
webster_full: OUTLANDISH, foreign; belonging to another country; not native.
From Old English ūtlendisc, “of an out-land.”
The modern sense of “bizarre, absurd” is a later drift of the word.
A KJV hapax: outlandish women caused Solomon to sin (Neh 13:26).
Nehemiah names the sin as marrying strange wives against the covenant (Neh 13:27).
scriptures: Did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things? yet among many nations was there no king like him, who was beloved of his God, and God made him king over all Israel: nevertheless even him did outlandish women cause to sin.
Shall we then hearken unto you to do all this great evil, to transgress against our God in marrying strange wives?
Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?
Rut 1:16

And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:
corruption_summary: The KJV word for foreign; it recovers Nehemiah’s warning against the unequal yoke — a covenant matter, never a matter of blood or nation.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption here is the abuse of Nehemiah’s text for ethnic separatism, and it must be named and refused outright. Men have taken “outlandish women” and the strange wives of Ezra and Nehemiah and made of them a charter for keeping the peoples apart by blood — as though God’s objection to Solomon’s wives were their ancestry. It was not. It was their altars. “His wives turned away his heart after other gods,” and Nehemiah names the sin exactly: “to transgress against our God in marrying strange wives.” Scripture’s own witnesses settle it. Ruth was a Moabitess and is in the line of David and of Christ, because she said, “thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.” Rahab was a Canaanite of Jericho and is named in the genealogy and in the roll of faith. The daughters of Moab were not shut out by blood; they were shut out by Chemosh, and when a Moabitess renounced Chemosh she was a daughter of Israel. Biblical anthropology knows two families only: one in Adam, where all fell, and one in Christ, where there is neither Jew nor Greek. Any reading that makes nation or lineage the boundary of the covenant is a corruption of the text it quotes.

The principle to recover, then, is the unequal yoke as Scripture actually draws it — between faith and unbelief, light and darkness, Christ and Belial. Solomon is the warning God chose: wisest of men, beloved of his God, unequalled among kings, and his heart was turned by the women he loved until it was not perfect with the LORD. If him, then whom? A believer who marries an unbeliever has not merely chosen a hard road; he has yoked his soul to an altar not his own and given his children a mother or a father who will teach them another god. The rule is not that a Christian must marry his own kind of people. The rule is that he must marry in the Lord — and by that rule a Moabitess who fears the LORD is a fitter wife than a daughter of Judah who does not.
roots_summary: The word means foreign, of another land — the KJV sense, older than the modern “bizarre.”
roots_lines: Outlandish — Old English ūtlendisc, “of a foreign land.”
From ūt (“out”) + land; hence not native, foreign.
The modern sense “bizarre” is a drift; the KJV means only foreign.
A KJV hapax: outlandish women caused Solomon to sin (Neh 13:26).
The offence was the altar, not the ancestry — strange gods, not strange blood.
usage: Outlandish means foreign, not absurd: the outlandish women of Neh 13 were wives of other lands.
Even Solomon, wisest of men, was turned by outlandish wives — the yoke bends the strongest neck.
Ruth the Moabitess was outlandish by birth and a daughter of Israel by faith: the altar draws the line.

etymology: From the Old French rereward (riere, “behind,” + warde, “guard”) — the rear guard of an army, the company that marches last, gathers the stragglers, and covers the host from pursuit. It is the parent of the modern rearguard.
biblical_def: The rereward is the rear guard — the body of men who march at the back of the host, gathering up the weak and the lagging and standing between the column and whatever hunts it. In the order of the camp it was a named office: when Israel moved, the standard of Dan “set forward, which was the rereward of all the camps throughout their hosts” (Num 10:25), the last tribe out and the shield of every tribe before it. At Jericho, “the rereward came after the ark” while the armed men went before the priests (Jos 6:9), the whole procession guarded front and back. But the glory of the word is that God takes the office Himself. To a people coming out of Babylon, told they need not flee in panic as their fathers fled Egypt, Isaiah says: “For ye shall not go out with haste, nor go by flight: for the LORD will go before you; and the God of Israel will be your rereward” (Isa 52:12). Before and behind. He is the vanguard who opens the road and the rear guard who covers the retreat — and the Hebrew margin is sweeter still: He will gather you up. The rear guard is where the stragglers are, the footsore, the sick, the ones who cannot keep the pace; and that is exactly where the LORD walks. Isaiah says it twice: “thy righteousness shall go before thee; the glory of the LORD shall be thy rereward” (Isa 58:8). Here is the perseverance of the saints in a soldier’s word. No man in that column is lost, because the last man in it is God.
webster_summary: The rear guard of an army; the company that marches last, gathering the stragglers and covering the host from pursuit.
webster_full: REREWARD, the rear guard; the part of an army that marches in the rear.
From Old French riere (“behind”) and warde (“guard”); now rearguard.
Its office is to gather the stragglers and cover the host from pursuit.
Dan was the rereward of all the camps of Israel (Num 10:25).
The LORD Himself is the rereward of His people (Isa 52:12).
scriptures: For ye shall not go out with haste, nor go by flight: for the LORD will go before you; and the God of Israel will be your rereward.
Isa 58:8
Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily: and thy righteousness shall go before thee; the glory of the LORD shall be thy rereward.
And the standard of the camp of the children of Dan set forward, which was the rereward of all the camps throughout their hosts: and over his host was Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai.
Jos 6:9
And the armed men went before the priests that blew with the trumpets, and the rereward came after the ark, the priests going on, and blowing with the trumpets.
corruption_summary: The army’s rear guard; it recovers the preservation of the saints — God goes before His people and behind them, and gathers up the stragglers.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the fear that God leads His people out and leaves them to keep up. Israel went out of Egypt in haste, with the dough unleavened and the enemy at their heels; but Isaiah promises a better exodus — no haste, no flight, no panic in the column — because the LORD goes before and the God of Israel is the rereward. A host with God at the front will not be turned back; a host with God at the rear will not be picked off. The believer who thinks himself safe only while he is strong has read the promise at one end. Grace opens the road ahead, and grace walks behind him where the danger follows.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is where the rear guard walks. It walks with the stragglers — the footsore, the wounded, the slow, the ones the column has left behind — and Isaiah’s margin reads that the LORD will gather you up. That is the doctrine of perseverance in a soldier’s word. The saints persevere because they are preserved; the weakest man in the march is covered by the glory of the LORD at his back. Christ loses none that the Father gave Him. Let the trembling believer take his comfort here: he is not the last man in the column. God is.
roots_summary: The word means the rear guard of an army — the company that marches last and covers the host.
roots_lines: Rereward — Old French riere (“behind”) + warde (“guard”).
It is the parent of the modern rearguard; not reward.
Its office is to gather the stragglers and cover the host from pursuit.
Dan marched as the rereward of all the camps (Num 10:25).
The LORD is the rereward of His people, going before and behind (Isa 52:12).
usage: The LORD will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rereward — vanguard and rear guard both.
Dan was the rereward of all the camps: the last standard out, the shield of every tribe before it.
The rereward walks where the stragglers are — which is why no saint in the column is lost.

etymology: A diminutive of the Old French targe, “a light shield,” from a Frankish root; hence a small shield or buckler carried on the arm. The modern sense — the mark one shoots at — arose only later, when shields were set up to be shot at in practice.
biblical_def: In the KJV a target is a shield. The word names a piece of defensive armour — a small shield or buckler borne before the body — and the modern reader must reverse his instinct to read it rightly. We hear target and think of the thing aimed at: the mark, the bullseye, the object of attack. The KJV means the thing held before you: the guard, the cover, the plate that takes the blow. The word’s history explains the reversal — old shields were set up as marks for archery practice, and in time the name of the shield passed to the mark it was used for, until the defence became the object of assault. Scripture shows the target in three lights. It is a giant’s armour: Goliath “had greaves of brass upon his legs, and a target of brass between his shoulders” (1Sa 17:6), and all that brass availed him nothing against a boy with a sling and the name of the LORD of hosts. It is a king’s treasure: “king Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold: six hundred shekels of gold went to one target” (1Ki 10:16) — shields too precious to fight with, hung in the house of the forest of Lebanon for glory, and carried off by Shishak within a generation. And it is a godly king’s honest war-gear: Asa had three hundred thousand men of Judah that bare targets and spears (2Ch 14:8), and with them he cried to the LORD and was heard. Above all three stands Paul’s word: “Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked” (Eph 6:16).
webster_summary: A shield or buckler borne on the arm — the thing held before you, not the thing aimed at.
webster_full: TARGET, a shield or buckler; a piece of defensive armour borne before the body.
A diminutive of Old French targe, “a light shield.”
The later sense — a mark to shoot at — came from shields set up for archery practice.
Goliath wore a target of brass between his shoulders (1Sa 17:6).
Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold for the house of the forest (1Ki 10:16).
scriptures: And he had greaves of brass upon his legs, and a target of brass between his shoulders.
And king Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold: six hundred shekels of gold went to one target.

And Asa had an army of men that bare targets and spears, out of Judah three hundred thousand; and out of Benjamin, that bare shields and drew bows, two hundred and fourscore thousand: all these were mighty men of valour.
Eph 6:16
Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked.
corruption_summary: A word that has turned inside out: the KJV’s target is the shield you hold, while ours is the mark you shoot at — defence become object of attack.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a genuine reversal, and it is worth naming plainly because it trips every modern reader of 1Sa 17:6. A target in the Authorized Version is a shield. Our target is a bullseye. The one is what covers you; the other is what is shot at. The drift happened honestly enough — men set old shields on posts and shot at them for practice, and the name of the armour slid over to the mark — but the result is that a word which once meant protection now means prey. A reader who does not know it will picture Goliath with a bullseye between his shoulders rather than a plate of brass, and will miss the point: the giant was armoured head to heel and still fell, because no target of brass turns the stone that God sends.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that honest drift of language. The principle to recover is which target a man trusts. Goliath had one of brass and died in it. Solomon made two hundred of beaten gold, six hundred shekels apiece — too costly to carry into any battle, hung on the wall for show — and Shishak king of Egypt took every one of them away, and Rehoboam replaced them with brass. That is the fate of every golden target: the glory a man hangs on his wall is carried off by the next invader. Asa’s three hundred thousand bore honest targets and spears, and when the Ethiopian host came out against him he cried, “LORD, it is nothing with thee to help,” and the LORD smote them. The armour is not nothing; but the arm is everything. Above all, take the shield of faith.
roots_summary: The word means a shield or buckler borne before the body — not the mark shot at.
roots_lines: Target — a diminutive of Old French targe, “a light shield.”
In the KJV it always means a shield, never a mark to aim at.
The modern sense arose from shields set up as marks for archery.
Goliath’s target was of brass; Solomon’s were of beaten gold.
The believer’s target is the shield of faith, quenching fiery darts (Eph 6:16).
usage: A target of brass between his shoulders: the KJV’s target is armour, not a bullseye.
Solomon’s golden targets never turned a blow — and Shishak carried every one of them away.
Asa’s men bore targets and spears, and their king bore something better: a cry to the LORD.

etymology: From the Greek progignōskein, “to know beforehand” (pro, “before,” + gignōskein, “to know”), through the Latin prognosticare; hence one who foretells, a foreteller of things to come. In the KJV, the “monthly prognosticators” of Babylon are the astrologers who read the moons for omens.
biblical_def: A prognosticator is a foreteller — one who professes to know beforehand what is coming. The word occurs once, in Isaiah’s taunt over doomed Babylon, and it is set in a list of her whole diviner’s trade: “Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee” (Isa 47:13). The Hebrew margin is exact — men “that give knowledge concerning the months” — the almanac-makers who charted the new moons and sold their forecasts to a city that could not live without them. Isaiah’s mockery is not that their art is wicked only, but that it is empty: let them stand up and save thee. They cannot. Babylon is wearied in the multitude of her counsels (Isa 47:12), and evil shall come upon her which she shall not know from whence it riseth. Against this whole trade stands the God who alone owns the future: “Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure” (Isa 46:10). That is the only credential of deity Isaiah will accept. The Law had already fenced His people from every counterfeit of it — no diviner, no observer of times, no enchanter, no witch shall be found among you (Deu 18:10) — and the prophet gives the rule that ends every argument: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: A foreteller of things to come; in Isaiah, the monthly almanac-diviners of Babylon who read the moons for omens.
webster_full: PROGNOSTICATOR, one who foretells; a foreknower of future events.
From Latin prognosticare, from the Greek for “to know beforehand.”
A KJV hapax: the “monthly prognosticators” of Babylon (Isa 47:13).
The margin reads, they “that give knowledge concerning the months.”
Isaiah bids them stand up and save the city — and they cannot.
scriptures: Stand now with thine enchantments, and with the multitude of thy sorceries, wherein thou hast laboured from thy youth; if so be thou shalt be able to profit, if so be thou mayest prevail.
Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:
There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch,
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Babylon’s monthly diviners have never gone out of business: the horoscope has been made respectable, and a prophecy industry sells what Isaiah mocked.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is that we have made Babylon’s trade a hobby. The monthly prognosticators charted the moons and sold their forecasts, and Isaiah told a city to call them up and see if they could save her. Nothing has changed but the packaging. The horoscope column, the birth chart, the app that tells a woman which sign she should marry, the “just for fun” consultation of the stars — these are the same stargazers, now respectable, now printed beside the crossword. The Law does not grade them by sincerity: there shall not be found among you an observer of times, an enchanter, a diviner. And Jeremiah says, “Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven.” God made the stars for signs and seasons, not for counsel. To read the sky for your future is to ask the creature a question only the Creator can answer, and to be dismayed at what the creature says is to fear a thing that cannot save.

The second corruption wears a Christian coat, and it must be named as plainly as the first. This dictionary is cessationist: the canon is closed, and the sign-gifts that authenticated the apostles ceased with them. The modern prophecy industry — the New Apostolic Reformation with its restored apostles and prophets, Bethel, IHOP, the “prophetic word” conference circuit and its personal words for a price — is the monthly prognosticator with a Bible on the table. It sells foreknowledge, which belongs to God alone; its forecasts fail and are quietly forgotten, exactly as Isaiah said they would; and Deuteronomy’s test for a prophet has no category for a man who is right sometimes. The remedy is Isaiah’s: to the law and to the testimony. God has declared the end from the beginning in a book, His counsel shall stand, and He will do all His pleasure. A Christian who wants to know the future has a Bible; a Christian who wants to know his own future has a Providence he is not permitted to read and a Father he is commanded to trust.
roots_summary: The word means a foreteller, one who professes to know things beforehand.
roots_lines: Prognosticator — from Greek pro (“before”) + gignōskein (“to know”).
Through Latin prognosticare, “to foretell, to forecast.”
A KJV hapax: the monthly prognosticators of Babylon (Isa 47:13).
They were almanac-diviners who read the new moons for omens.
God alone declares the end from the beginning (Isa 46:10).
usage: Let the monthly prognosticators stand up and save thee — and Babylon fell in a night.
The horoscope is Babylon’s trade in a modern column: an observer of times is forbidden, not quaint.
God declares the end from the beginning; every other foreteller is guessing and charging for it.

etymology: From off + scouring — that which is scoured off in cleaning: the scrapings, the filth wiped from a vessel and thrown away. It renders the Greek peripsema, the dirt rubbed off all around, and the Hebrew of Lamentations for refuse and sweepings.
biblical_def: Offscouring is what is scraped off and thrown out — the scourings of a pot, the filth wiped from a dish, the refuse no one keeps. It is the lowest word a man can use of himself, and Paul uses it of the apostles. Cataloguing what the ministry had cost them — hunger, thirst, nakedness, buffeting, homelessness, labour with their own hands — he ends: “Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day” (1Co 4:13). He had already said God had set forth the apostles last, “as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men” (1Co 4:9). Note the sting in the context: he wrote it to a church that thought itself full, rich, reigning as kings — wise, strong, honourable in its own eyes — while the men who brought them the gospel were the world’s garbage. Jeremiah had wept the same word over Zion: “Thou hast made us as the offscouring and refuse in the midst of the people” (Lam 3:45). And the word has a Master. Christ was despised and rejected, cast out of the city as a thing unclean, and so the writer to the Hebrews calls the church after Him: “Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13). Outside the camp is where the ashes were carried and the refuse burned; it is also where the Lord of glory hung. The offscouring of all things is not an accident of the apostolic age. It is the uniform.
webster_summary: That which is scoured off; the scrapings, refuse, or filth of a thing — used by Paul of the apostles themselves.
webster_full: OFFSCOURING, that which is scoured off; refuse; the filth wiped away and cast out.
From off and scour; it renders the Greek peripsema, dirt rubbed off all around.
It is the meanest thing a man can be called, and Paul owns it (1Co 4:13).
Jeremiah laments that Zion was made the offscouring in the midst of the people (Lam 3:45).
The apostles were a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men (1Co 4:9).
scriptures: Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day.
Lam 3:45
Thou hast made us as the offscouring and refuse in the midst of the people.
For I think that God hath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men.
Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
corruption_summary: Paul’s word for the apostles: the world’s garbage. It stands squarely against a religion of platforms, brands, and prosperity.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the exact inversion of this word by the prosperity-and-platform religion of our day. Paul says the apostles were set forth last, appointed to death, a spectacle to the world, the filth of it, the offscouring of all things — and he says it in deliberate contrast to a Corinthian church that was full, rich, and reigning as kings without them. That contrast has been resolved the wrong way. The modern teacher measures his calling by his following, his book sales, his jet, his brand; he preaches a Christ who will make you full, rich, and reigning now; and he holds up the very things Paul held up as evidence that Corinth had misunderstood the gospel. If the apostolic ministry looked like offscouring and the modern ministry looks like Corinth, it is not the apostles who need explaining.

The principle to recover is that shame borne for Christ is the pattern, not the exception. Christ was led outside the city as an unclean thing, to the place where the refuse was burned, and the writer to the Hebrews draws the only conclusion: let us go forth therefore unto Him without the camp, bearing His reproach. The camp has the crowds, the honour, and the applause; the Lord is outside it. A servant is not greater than his master, and the disciple who is never counted the offscouring of anything should ask whether he has followed his Lord out of the gate at all. This is no counsel of despair — being defamed, Paul says, we intreat; he answered slander with entreaty and reproach with the gospel. But it is the sober arithmetic of discipleship: the men who turned the world upside down were, in the world’s ledger, its garbage, and they reckoned the trade a bargain.
roots_summary: The word means that which is scoured off — scrapings, refuse, the filth cast out.
roots_lines: Offscouring — from off + scouring, what is scraped away.
It renders the Greek peripsema, the dirt rubbed off all around a vessel.
It names the refuse of the world, the thing no one keeps.
Paul calls the apostles the offscouring of all things (1Co 4:13).
Zion was made the offscouring in the midst of the people (Lam 3:45).
usage: We are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things — the apostles’ uniform.
Corinth reigned as kings while the men who brought them Christ were counted the world’s refuse.
Christ was cast without the camp: go forth unto Him there, bearing His reproach.
